title: A lap's rot is the body-rate integral, so the craft's BANK silently splits the loop's own single rotation between pitch and yaw; past 41 degrees of bank a Powerloop is named Donkey Loop
problem:
closePath builds rot as lastRot - startRot, where totalTurns[k] (line 1960-1962) is the plain time integral of the BODY rate about body axis k. Body axes tumble with the craft, so this integral is not "turns about each axis": it is the projection of the craft's actual rotation onto a frame that is itself rotating. For the loop family the leakage is not a subtle second-order holonomy term, it is a first-order DC term with a closed form.

Fly a Powerloop: the craft's attitude must rotate exactly once about the RAIL's axis to keep the nose tangent through the circle. Let phi be the craft's roll about its own nose axis measured from wings-parallel-to-the-rail. The nose is tangent, so the rail axis is perpendicular to body x and the roll integral stays ~0; but the rail axis sits at angle phi in the body y / body z plane, so the gyro sees q = Omega*cos(phi) and r = Omega*sin(phi). The integral reads rot = [0, cos(phi), sin(phi)] turns, with rot_pitch^2 + rot_yaw^2 = 1. The pilot never touched the yaw stick and the craft never changed heading in any world sense.

A banked powerloop is ordinary flying, not a mistake: the craft slides ALONG the rail while it loops around it, and stepOneLap (line 2064-2075) projects the along-axis component out, so that drift is invisible to the lap and the winding still reads a clean whole turn. The lap is a textbook Powerloop by geometry and by eye; only the gyro integral disagrees.

Now walk the pattern table (Powerloop line 664 rot pitch 1, Maverick Loop line 669 rot pitch 0, Donkey Loop line 829 rot pitch 0.5 yaw 1) against matchSteps line 3164-3176, where err <= 0.25 is free, err <= 0.5 costs 1 slack, SLACK_MAX is 2, and bestMatch (line 2896) breaks a length-and-slack tie on PRICE:
  phi = 0    pitch 1.00 yaw 0.00  Powerloop slack 0                      -> Powerloop (200)
  phi = 30   pitch 0.87 yaw 0.50  Powerloop slack 0, Donkey slack 2      -> Powerloop
  phi = 45   pitch 0.71 yaw 0.71  Powerloop slack 1, Donkey slack 1      -> Donkey Loop (600), on price
  phi = 60   pitch 0.50 yaw 0.87  Powerloop slack 1, Donkey slack 0      -> Donkey Loop
  phi = 75   pitch 0.26 yaw 0.97  Powerloop rejected, Donkey slack 0     -> Donkey Loop
  phi = 90   pitch 0.00 yaw 1.00  Maverick slack 0, Donkey slack 1       -> Maverick Loop (100)
The crossover is exact: Powerloop stays clean while cos(phi) >= 0.75, i.e. phi <= 41.4 degrees. Above 41.4 degrees of bank the same flown shape is a Donkey Loop, and at 90 it is a Maverick Loop. This is precisely the reported Jump Rope rail lap coming out Powerloop / Donkey Loop / Maverick Loop on different runs, and it is also why Donkey Loop, which the Tricktionary defines by a deliberate 360 yaw spin at the top, can be scored for 600 points by a pilot who never yawed.

The same mechanism runs the other way and explains Cinnamon Roll coming out Mavvy Roll. A heading rotation (world-vertical spin) flown at pitch attitude theta reads body yaw cos(theta) and body ROLL -sin(theta). Cinnamon Roll's slow 360 heading spin, flown while the craft is nose-up climbing one side of the bar, leaks into the roll integral; at an average 60 degrees of pitch attitude it reads yaw 0.5 and roll 0.87, and Mavvy Roll (line 823, rot pitch 0, roll 1) is a one-step pattern that matches that with slack 0.

So the answer to the dimension question is: no, rot is not a measurable quantity. Its value depends on the craft's orientation about the flown path, which is a free parameter that no trick in the catalogue names, and the pattern table treats its three components as if they were independent counts of flips, rolls and yaw spins.
scenario: Pilot flies a clean Powerloop around a city rail, entering with about 45 degrees of bank because the rail sits diagonal to the approach, and slides a couple of metres along the rail through the loop. The lap winds 1.00 turn about the rail axis from under to under, so turns and startSide are right. rot comes out [~0, 0.71, 0.71]. Powerloop spends 1 slack on pitch err 0.29; Donkey Loop spends 1 slack on yaw err 0.29 and nothing on pitch err 0.21. Equal length, equal slack, so bestMatch takes the dearer: Donkey Loop, 600 points, for a trick the pilot did not fly. Repeat the same loop with the wings closer to the rail and it is a Powerloop for 200. Nothing about the trick changed except a bank angle the pattern never asks about.
fix:
Stop resolving a lap's concurrent rotation in the body frame and resolve it in a frame fixed to the LAP, keeping the integral (counting is still right: a quaternion difference cannot tell 360 from 720).

main.js already has everything needed. At src/main.js:5133 it builds scoreQuat, the body-to-world rotation in the obstacles' own frame, and derives scoreFwd from it. Extend the step() ABI to carry that quaternion (or, cheaper, the three world-frame body axis vectors) alongside the rates, and in step() form the world angular velocity omega_w = R * [p, q, r].

In stepOneLap, where ob.dx/dy/dz is already in hand, build an orthonormal triad fixed to the lap: a_hat = the obstacle axis; u_hat = normalize(worldUp - (worldUp . a_hat) a_hat); c_hat = a_hat x u_hat. sideOf (line 2296-2302) already assumes a bar is horizontal, so this triad is always well conditioned for the tricks that use rot. Accumulate three turn counts instead of the body triple:
    spin    += (omega_w . a_hat) * dt / TURN     turns about the rail's own axis
    heading += (omega_w . u_hat) * dt / TURN     turns about world up
    cross   += (omega_w . c_hat) * dt / TURN
Keep the existing body-roll integral as the fourth number: the loop's rotation is perpendicular to the nose, so body roll never picks up the bank leakage and a roll is already measured correctly.

Carry [spin, heading, roll] on the path primitive in place of rot, snapshot them in PathRun.snapshot the same way histRot is snapshotted today, and re-express every rot term on a `path` step. The rewrites are mechanical:
    Powerloop            spin 1,   heading 0
    Maverick Loop        spin 0,   heading 0
    Power Flip           spin 2
    Power Roll           spin 1,   roll 1        (roll unchanged)
    Inverted 360 PL      spin 1,   heading 1
    Donkey Loop          spin 0.5, heading 1
    Barani / Mavani      spin 1 / 0.5, heading 0.5
    Cinnamon Roll        spin 0,   heading 1
    Jump Rope            spin 0,   roll 0
    Mavvy Roll           spin 0,   roll 1
    Immelmann / Matty Flip / Split-S / Beginner Matty / Anti Matty / Power Matty: the half-lap `pitch` term becomes the same number of `spin`; their `roll` terms are unchanged
    Matty 360            spin 0.5, heading 1
    Split Yaw            spin 0.5, roll 0.5, heading 0.5
    Matty Roll           spin 0.75, roll 1
What keeps working untouched: every pure-rotation pattern (Roll, Flip, Yaw Spin, Rubik's Cube, Segmented, Snapback, Eject Roll, Inverted Yaw Tracking) never reads a lap's rot; every pole pattern (Orbit, Trippy Spin) has no rot term; and every `roll` term on a lap step keeps its present meaning and its present numbers. What has to be re-expressed is exactly the `pitch` and `yaw` terms on `path` steps, about thirty of them, all listed above.

Say plainly in the comment what this does and does not buy. It is still a time integral, so it is still not a group-theoretic net rotation; what changes is that the frame no longer tumbles with the craft, so the always-present bank term vanishes and the integral is exact whenever the rotations composing the trick share an axis, which for the loop family they do.

If the ABI change is refused for now, the only honest stopgap is to stop asking the question the integral cannot answer: replace the pitch and yaw terms with the single invariant sqrt(pitch^2 + yaw^2), which is stable under bank and separates Maverick Loop (0), Powerloop (1) and Power Flip (2) reliably. That removes the wrong answers at the price of retiring Donkey Loop, Inverted 360 Powerloop, Barani and Mavani, which cannot be told apart on it at all. Better a trick that is not named than a trick that is named wrong.

title: rot's window is the lap plus a fixed 800 ms of whatever came before it, and how much of that 800 ms exists depends on approach speed and on when the previous lap closed
problem:
When the winding gate opens, the run backdates itself to the OLDEST entry in its ring buffer (PathRun.snapshot, line 1641) and takes startRot from there, not from the moment the lap began. PATH_LOOKBACK is 800, so rot's window is [gate - 800 ms, high-water mark] and the gate itself opens about a fifth of the way into the loop. rot therefore always charges the lap with several hundred milliseconds of rotation flown BEFORE the craft ever started going round.

The backdate is right for winding and for startSide, which is the argument written at PATH_LOOKBACK (line 483): the extra winding over the ramp is small and the side is topological. It does not carry over to rotation, because rotation is not small over 800 ms. Betaflight's default yaw rate is well over 400 deg/s; 800 ms of it is a whole turn. Whatever the pilot did with the sticks in the second before committing to the loop is added to the trick's identity.

Worse, the length of that window is not constant. run.reset() clears the history the millisecond the obstacle enters the engaged set (pathStep line 2053-2056), and closePath calls run.clearHistory() (line 2404), so histFill starts from zero at each of those. REACH for a bar is 12 m (src/game/obstacles.js:125). The pre-lap rotation charged to a lap is therefore min(800 ms, 12/v seconds, time since the last lap on that rail closed). Entering at 12 m/s gives the full 800 ms; entering at 20 m/s gives 600 ms; on the second pass of a jump rope it is whatever the cadence happens to be. On the same stick input a 200 ms difference in that window is 0.25 turns of yaw at ordinary rates, which is exactly CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE, i.e. exactly enough to move the lap from one pattern's accept band into another's.

And the rotation inside the backdate is counted twice. Rotations are held by a lap only if they close while the path run is already open (closeRun line 2612-2618); one that closes before the gate opens stays in pending and is matched and scored as its own primitive, while its turns are simultaneously inside the lap's rot.
scenario: Pilot yaw-spins 360 to line up on a rail, then immediately flies a plain Powerloop, entering at 12 m/s. The yaw run closes before the winding gate opens, so it stays in pending. The gate opens ~400 ms into the loop; the backdate reaches 800 ms before that, i.e. ~400 ms before the loop began, and swallows most of the line-up spin. The lap's rot reads pitch ~1, yaw ~1. drain names the yaw primitive first as a Yaw Spin, then matches the lap alone against the one-step patterns: Inverted 360 Powerloop (line 771, rot pitch 1 yaw 1) matches with slack 0 and pays 650, against Powerloop's 200. The pilot is paid twice for the spin and paid at Master rate for a Novice trick. Fly the identical pair of motions arriving at 22 m/s and the ring buffer only holds ~550 ms, the spin falls outside the window, the lap reads pitch 1 yaw ~0.3, and it is a Powerloop for 200. Same sticks, same shape, different name, decided by approach speed.
fix:
Split the two windows, because they answer different questions. Keep the 800 ms backdate for startWind and startSide, which is what it was argued for. Take startRot from the moment the LAP began, not from the oldest snapshot.

Concretely: the lap's rotation window should open where the winding actually starts, not where the ring buffer happens to end. Walk back through the snapshot ring from the gate to the first entry whose winding is still monotonic in dirSign and whose |wind - windTotal| is under, say, a sixteenth of a turn, and take startRot from THAT entry; that is the point the craft committed to going round, and it is bounded by the lap rather than by a wall-clock constant. Fall back to the gate's own totals when the ring has nothing older, so a short history under-reports rather than mis-reports.

Then close the double count: at closePath, subtract from rot the turns of any primitive still sitting in this.pending whose [startMs, endMs] lies inside the rot window, or hold it the way heldByPath holds a rotation that closed during the lap. One motion must be charged to one trick, which is the rule sameMotionLap and absorbedByLap already enforce for laps and for rotations inside laps; the backdate window is the one place it is not enforced.

Either way, record the rot window's actual length on the primitive so a diagnostic can show it. A window whose length varies with approach speed is not something a pilot can ever be told about.

title: The rot accept band with slack is exactly as wide as the spacing between the loop-family classes, so adjacent tricks always overlap and price decides
problem:
matchSteps accepts a rot axis free when err <= CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE (0.25) and at a cost of 1 slack when err <= CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE + SLACK_ROT (0.5), with SLACK_MAX 2. But the pattern table quantises rot in quarter and half turns: on pitch the loop family's classes are 0 (Maverick Loop), 0.5 (Donkey Loop, Mavani), 1 (Powerloop, Anti Matty), 1.5 (Power Matty), 2 (Power Flip). The class spacing is 0.5 and the accept half-width with slack is also 0.5, so every class's slack band reaches the CENTRE of both its neighbours. The free band alone is +/-0.25, exactly half the spacing, which tiles the axis perfectly with no overlap; SLACK_ROT doubles it and destroys that partition.

bestMatch (line 2896) breaks ties on length, then slack, then PRICE. So wherever two neighbouring classes both match at the same slack, the dearer trick wins by construction rather than by evidence. The exact midpoint is the clearest case: a lap reading pitch 0.75 sits err 0.25 from both 0.5 and 1.0, so both are free, both slack 0, and Donkey Loop's 600 beats Powerloop's 200. A real flight sits on that line often, because 0.75 is what a loop flown with 41 degrees of bank produces (see finding 1), and because HALF_LAP_MIN's own comment says a flown lap reads short.

This is independent of the frame question. Even with a perfectly measurable rot, a tolerance as wide as the spacing means the loop family cannot be partitioned, and the tie-break hands every ambiguous reading to whichever trick the catalogue prices highest.
scenario: A lap from under a rail, one whole turn, reads rot pitch 0.75 and yaw 0.66. Powerloop: pitch err 0.25, free, slack 0. Donkey Loop: pitch err 0.25 free, yaw err 0.34, costs 1, slack 1. Powerloop wins here. Nudge the same flight to pitch 0.70 / yaw 0.71 and Powerloop pays 1 for pitch while Donkey pays 1 for yaw: equal length, equal slack, and 600 beats 200. A five hundredth of a turn changes a 200 point Novice trick into a 600 point Master trick, and it changes it in the direction that pays more, which is the direction nobody reports as a bug.
fix:
Make rot a nearest-class assignment rather than a per-axis band test. Either set SLACK_ROT to 0, so the accept half-width is 0.25, exactly half the 0.5 class spacing, and the classes partition the axis cleanly with no overlap; or, better, before running the pattern loop, snap each rot component to the nearest quarter turn and require an exact match, refusing the lap outright when the reading sits within a small epsilon of a class boundary. Refusing is the right behaviour there: a lap that is genuinely halfway between a Powerloop and a Donkey Loop is not either of them, and the file's own rule is that a trick it cannot name is not scored rather than scored as something else.

If slack on rot is kept at all, it must not be spendable by a pattern whose price is higher than the competing exact reading's. The cheapest guard is to make the tie-break prefer the pattern with the smaller total rot error before it looks at price, so tolerance can never buy a dearer name.

title: Every [rotation, lap] pattern is unreachable when the entry rotation closes while any path run is open, and the primitive is then destroyed
problem: The pending buffer is ordered by CLOSURE order, not flight order, and closeRun() diverts any rotation that closes while `anyPathOpen()` into `heldByPath` instead of pending (2617-2620). closePath() then copies heldByPath into the lap primitive as `held` (2400) and clears it. Those held rotations are handed back ONLY if the lap names nothing (drain, 2683-2691); when the lap IS named, emit() splices the lap out (2762) and never looks at `u.held`, so they are silently discarded. A path run opens on PATH_RATE_ON 0.08 turns/s plus PATH_TANGENT_ON 2.5 m/s with `circling` (2124), which any flypast of a lamp post or fence post at flying speed satisfies, and up to MAX_PATH_RUNS 32 of them can be live at once in a town with 886 poles. So whether the entry rotation of a pattern reaches pending at all is decided by whether some unrelated post happened to be in reach at that millisecond. Twelve patterns are gated on this: Jump Rope (986), Cinnamon Roll (995), Side Loop (1004), Blindflip (776), Matty Twister (895), Half Matty (905), 540 Half Matty, Stellar Eject Roll, True Barani, Rollani, Flipani, Mavvelmann.
scenario: Jump Rope on a rail: pilot yaws 90 degrees, then flies a flat whole lap from under. If the quarter yaw closes while nothing is being wound, pending = [yaw 0.25, lap] and Jump Rope matches at two steps. If a fence post beside the rail was being wound at that instant (tangent > 2.5 m/s, radial small, so `circling` is true), the yaw goes to heldByPath, the rail lap is pushed alone, pending = [lap], the two-step patterns are all unreachable, and the winner is chosen from the one-step lap family by the rot drift alone: Maverick Loop, Powerloop or Donkey Loop. That is exactly the reported FLAKY 1/2 'Jump Rope rail lap named Powerloop / Donkey Loop / Maverick Loop on different runs'. Cinnamon Roll fails the same way: its entry quarter yaw is swallowed, the lap is left with pitch ~0 and a roll integral near 1, and the one-step winner is Mavvy Roll (250) over Maverick Loop (100), which is the reported 0/2 'comes out Mavvy Roll'. The yaw is also destroyed rather than returned, so the pilot is not even paid the building block.
fix: Split the two jobs the `anyPathOpen()` test is currently doing. In closeRun (2617) only divert a rotation into heldByPath if it actually lies inside an open lap: apply the same 50% overlap test absorbedByLap uses (2450) against the open run's [startMs, nowMs], so a rotation that finished before the lap opened stays in pending. Second, insert into pending by startMs rather than pushing, so buffer order is flight order regardless of which run closed first. Third, in emit() (2762), before discarding a named lap, hand back any prim in `used[i].held` that fails absorbedByLap against the lap's own window instead of dropping it on the floor.

title: A lap pattern that omits a rot axis can never win a tie against its own superset, so Powerloop and Maverick Loop are unnameable whenever drift lands in the superset's band
problem: matchSteps only checks the axes a pattern names (3167-3178), so a pattern naming a strict superset of another's axes is strictly LESS permissive but never costs more slack when the extra axis happens to land within CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE (0.25) of its target. bestMatch (2913-2919) compares length, then slack, then price, so the superset ties on slack and wins on price, always: every superset in this file is dearer than its subset. Powerloop {pitch:1} 200 is a subset of Power Roll {pitch:1, roll:1} 450 and of Inverted 360 Powerloop {pitch:1, yaw:1} 650; Maverick Loop {pitch:0} 100 is a subset of Mavvy Roll {pitch:0, roll:1} 250. The comment at 750 defends this as 'the pilot did roll', which is only true if rot were a measurement of intent. It is the time integral of body rates over a lap, so the roll and yaw entries of a pure pitch loop are holonomy and pilot correction, not a roll.
scenario: Sweeping the drift plane with the matcher's own rules: a Powerloop flown with pitch integral exactly 1.0 is named 'Powerloop' on 100% of the plane while roll and yaw drift stay under 0.6 turns, on 86% at drift up to 0.8, and on only 46% at drift up to 1.5 (the rest split 32% Inverted 360 Powerloop, 22% Power Roll). The failure is not gradual: as soon as |yaw| reaches 0.75 the name is Inverted 360 Powerloop, a 650 point Master trick, at zero slack, for a pilot who never touched yaw; below 0.75 it is Powerloop at 200. The same lap with |roll| in [0.75,1.25] is Power Roll at 450. A Maverick Loop with roll drift in that band is Mavvy Roll at 250 instead of 100, which with finding 1 is the whole of the Cinnamon Roll failure. The reported Donkey Loop naming proves these bands are reached in real flight: Donkey Loop cannot match at all unless the lap's yaw integral was already in [0.5,1.5].
fix: Make superset wins require positive evidence rather than the absence of a constraint. Either (a) in bestMatch, when two candidates tie on length and slack, prefer the one whose named axes are a superset ONLY if every extra axis matched within CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE/2 (0.125) rather than the full 0.25, so a drift sitting at the edge of the band cannot buy the dearer name; or (b) give every member of a lap family an explicit target on all three axes (Powerloop gains roll:0, yaw:0; Maverick Loop gains roll:0, yaw:0) so the comparison is like for like and the slack test decides it. (b) is the one that also fixes finding 3 and is what the family comment at 745-752 declines to do.

title: Adjacent rot targets are spaced 0.5 apart with a 0.25 half-width, so the lap families tile the axis with no dead band and the name flips at an exact quarter turn, always toward the dearer trick
problem: The rot test is `err > CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE` with CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE 0.25 (507), and the family targets are 0.5 apart, so the zero-slack acceptance windows abut exactly and SLACK_ROT (0.25) makes them overlap by half a turn at cost 1. There is no dead band and no hysteresis anywhere: every value of the pitch integral names some trick, and at the shared edge both neighbours score zero slack, so the price tie break at 2918 hands the boundary to the trick with MORE rotation, which is always the dearer one. Driving the matcher's own rules across the axis gives, for a half lap from over: Beginner Matty below 0.25, Matty Flip to 0.75, Anti Matty to 1.25, Power Matty above; and for a whole lap from under: Maverick Loop below 0.50, Powerloop to 1.50, Power Flip above. Worse, the family is inconsistent about which axes it pins: Matty Flip (678) and Beginner Matty (683) pin roll to 0 while Anti Matty (874), Power Matty (879) and Matty 360 do not, and Split-S (673) pins roll to 0.5. So the cheap tricks pay slack for drift the dear ones are exempt from.
scenario: A flown Matty Flip has exactly one correct window and it is a quarter turn wide on roll: at roll drift 0 to 0.25 it is Matty Flip (200); from 0.25 it is Split-S (100, and it wins on SLACK, not price, because Split-S targets roll 0.5); from 0.75 it is Matty Roll (425). On pitch its window is [0.25, 0.75): a hair under 0.25 and it is Beginner Matty at 100, a hair over 0.75 and it is Anti Matty at 250. Over a modest drift square of +/-0.4 turns on roll and yaw the correct name comes out on only 62% of the plane, the rest Split-S and Split Yaw. That is the reported Matty Flip 0/2 ('Beginner Matty, or a 1.5 turn lap'). The Powerloop/Donkey Loop swap is the same edge: with yaw near 1, pitch 0.74 gives Donkey Loop and pitch 0.76 gives Inverted 360 Powerloop, and neither reading is ever Powerloop.
fix: Separate 'this trick' from 'not this trick'. Accept a rot axis at zero slack only within CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE/2 of the target, charge one slack point out to CONCURRENT_TOLERANCE, and REFUSE beyond it, so the quarter-turn strip between two family members names nothing instead of being reassigned to the neighbour. And pin the same axis set across a whole family (all of the over-half-lap patterns name roll and yaw, or none of them do), so a member cannot lose to a sibling merely because it was the only one that mentioned the axis the drift landed on.

title: Length beats cleanliness absolutely and no pattern bounds the gap between its steps, so two tricks flown seconds apart merge into one dearer name
problem: bestMatch tests `n > best.steps` before it ever looks at slack (2916), so a two-step pattern that missed two constraints by a full quarter turn each (slack 2, the SLACK_MAX ceiling) outranks a one-step pattern that matched exactly at slack 0. matchSteps imposes no upper bound on the time between consecutive primitives; the only thing that stops a stale primitive being joined to a later one is hold() (2949), which returns true unconditionally while `anyOpen() || anyPathOpen()`. As established in finding 1, a path run is open for much of ordinary flight in this town, so drain is blocked, primitives pile up, and the buffer is then matched greedily from the front with no notion of contiguity.
scenario: The most ordinary rail sequence there is: a Powerloop, then a Matty Flip rewind back under the same rail a second or two later. pending = [lap under 1 turn (pitch~1), lap over 0.5 turn (pitch~0.5)]. Barani (794) is [under 1 with rot{pitch:1, yaw:0.5}, over 0.5 with rot{pitch:0.5}]: two steps, so it beats Powerloop at any slack, and it matches whenever the first lap's yaw integral is anywhere in [0, 1.0] (zero slack in [0.25,0.75], one point out to 1.0). The pilot is paid 700 for a Master trick they did not fly, and the Matty Flip disappears into it. If the yaw drift misses, Power Split (785) picks it up instead whenever the second lap's roll integral lands in [0,1], for 300. And whether the merge happens at all is decided by whether an unrelated pole run in between reached PATH_MIN_TURNS (2319) and pushed a junk lap into the front of the buffer, which breaks the two-step prefix and lets the Powerloop emit on its own. Same flown shape, three possible names, selected by street furniture.
fix: Give matchSteps a contiguity rule: a step may not begin more than SETTLE_MS after the previous step's endMs plus whatever stallMs/gapMs that step explicitly asks for (emit already computes exactly this quantity as `dead` at 2778-2790, but only uses it to grade). Reject the pattern rather than grading it SLOPPY. Separately, make hold() (2949) block only on path runs that could still claim a buffered primitive, i.e. runs that opened before the newest pending primitive closed, instead of on any open run anywhere.
